v.why: Adding the input-to-output residual where none exists restores gradient flow and yields much larger gains than replacing an existing conv/pool on that edge.
With edge 1->3 absent, node 3 has fewer inputs, so a direct skip into the output matters more.
Filling the empty 0->3 edge creates a short path to the output, while replacing an existing op barely changes the cell.
Adding a new conv path into the output node helps much more than swapping an op that already feeds it.
When edge 2->3 is missing, edge 1->3 is the only conv route to the output, so adding a conv there gives large gains.
Without the 0->3 skip, a skip on 2->3 supplies the missing residual path; otherwise it just replaces a useful conv.
Adding a conv on a missing edge into the output adds both capacity and connectivity, whereas replacing an existing op only changes the op type.
Removing a parameterized 3x3 conv on 0->1 loses more capacity than removing a parameter-free skip or pool.
When edge 2->3 is absent, edge 1->3 is a main path into the output, so degrading it to pooling hurts more.
When the cell already has a 3x3 conv on 0->1, another conv on 0->2 adds little, unlike in conv-poor cells.

raw:
These hypotheses come from two sources: the 100 experiments, and the general pattern on NAS-Bench-201 that the edge 0→3 skip and the paths into node 3 matter most.

- **Edge 3 (input→output).** When this edge is `none`, the cell loses its direct residual path. Adding a skip_connect or a 1×1 conv there gives much larger gains (experiments 11, 14, 17–20, 92, 95–100) than replacing an existing conv or pool (12, 13, 93, 94). The gain is also larger when edge 4 is `none`, because node 3 then has fewer inputs (17, 19, 20).
- **Edge 4 (node 1→output).** Adding a 3×3 conv where the edge was `none` gives big gains (55, 58–60). Replacing an existing op gives almost nothing (52–54). The effect is strongest when edge 5 is also `none` (58, 59).
- **Edge 5 (node 2→output).** Replacing edge 5 with skip_connect helps only when edge 3 is `none`, because the skip then supplies the missing residual (72, 74 vs 71, 73, 75–79). Adding a 3×3 conv where edge 5 was `none` is reliably positive (1–3, 10).
- **Removing or degrading ops.** Removing a 3×3 conv on edge 0 hurts more than removing a skip or pool there (31–36 vs 37, 38). Turning edge 4 into avg_pool hurts badly when edge 5 is `none` (85, 86), since edge 4 is then a main path into the output.
- **Edge 1 (input→node 2).** A 3×3 conv on edge 1 adds little when edge 0 is already a 3×3 conv (41–47 vs 48–50).

The weakest hypotheses are the edge-1 one and the edge-4 / edge-5=`none` one. Each rests on only a few experiments, and the edge-1 rule is clearer on C100 and IN16 than on C10. The two all-skip and all-pool parents (15, 16) go against the edge-3 skip rule, but those cells are degenerate.
